value.overview: The White-rumped Sandpiper (Calidris fuscicollis) is a long-winged shorebird that breeds in the high Arctic and migrates to South America. It is slightly larger and longer-winged than many other small “peep” sandpipers. Its most useful field mark is the bright white rump and lower back visible in flight. The species often travels in flocks with other shorebirds and undertakes one of the longest migrations of any North American bird.
value.classification: The White-rumped Sandpiper belongs to the sandpiper family Scolopacidae in the shorebird order Charadriiformes. It is one of the small migratory sandpipers in the genus Calidris.
value.identification: This is a medium-sized small sandpiper with a fairly long, slightly drooping bill, long pointed wings, and a relatively long body. Breeding-plumaged birds have brown, black, white, and rusty markings, with dark streaking across the breast and upperparts. Nonbreeding birds are plainer gray-brown, while juveniles have a scaly appearance. All ages show a distinctive white rump and pale lower back in flight, contrasting with the darker wings and tail. Its call is a high, squeaky note.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds across moist high-Arctic tundra from northeastern Alaska through northern Canada. During migration and the nonbreeding season it uses freshwater marshes, flooded fields, shallow ponds, muddy shorelines, lagoons, estuaries, tidal flats, riverbanks, and beaches. In Costa Rica, it is a migrant rather than a resident or breeding bird. It occurs mainly at suitable coastal and inland wetlands during passage, where it may join mixed flocks of other migratory shorebirds. It is generally uncommon and can be overlooked among similar species.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds breeding in the Arctic migrate south through the Americas to South America, with passage through Costa Rica during migration periods, especially in spring and fall. Costa Rica is not a regular breeding or established wintering area for the species.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in the high Arctic, usually in moist tundra near freshwater ponds, lakes, or streams, although some pairs nest in drier tundra. The nest is a shallow depression lined with plant material, placed on the ground among mosses, sedges, grasses, or low shrubs. The female usually lays four eggs. Males perform conspicuous flight and ground displays, including hovering or fluttering flights accompanied by unusual vocalizations. Both parents contribute to incubation, while the young are precocial and leave the nest soon after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: White-rumped Sandpipers feed mainly on small invertebrates, including insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, mollusks, and other aquatic or soil-dwelling prey. They forage by walking through shallow water, wet mud, moss, or short vegetation and probing repeatedly with the bill. In Costa Rica, migrants may feed along muddy margins of wetlands, estuaries, lagoons, and flooded fields. They sometimes forage in mixed shorebird flocks but may defend small feeding areas.
value.behavior: This species is active, social, and often encountered in flocks during migration. It commonly feeds by probing rapidly while walking, sometimes inserting the bill deeply into soft mud. Birds frequently rest together on open shorelines or shallow wetland edges. Its long, pointed wings produce a swift, direct flight, and the white rump is conspicuous when it takes off. On the breeding grounds, males perform elaborate aerial and ground displays. The species may make long nonstop flights during migration, particularly over the Atlantic.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered relatively large, but long-term and current trends are not well known. Available evidence suggests that monitoring is insufficient to determine a precise global trend.
